title: Natural gas leak
aliases: I smell natural gas in my house
tldr: If you smell gas or suspect a leak, leave the area on foot immediately. Do not use switches, flames, phones or engines in the suspected leak area. Once safely away, call emergency services and your gas utility. Do not reenter until cleared.
steps: Do not search for the leak or stop to collect belongings.
Do not turn electrical devices on or off, light flames, operate garage doors or start a vehicle nearby.
Give the address and what you noticed to emergency services and the utility.
Wait outside the danger area and follow responder instructions.
next: Have the utility or a qualified technician restore service and inspect appliances when required.
watch: Never use a flame to test for leaks or attempt your own repair.
review_status: source-linked editorial review; not independent expert certification
without_help: Stay outside and away even if the utility line is busy. Keep others from entering without approaching the leak. A lack of response does not make reentry safe; use another place to stay until the hazard has been assessed by qualified personnel.
household: Use a short instruction everyone can follow: leave together by the nearest safe route. Include people who cannot smell well, hear an alarm or move independently. Keep the meeting point away from the suspected gas area.
pack_now: Prioritize supplies named in this guide that are usable by the person who needs them. Keep the checklist and relevant contact details accessible. Check carrying capacity, storage and equipment instructions in advance; collecting equipment must not delay the immediate protective action.
faqs: Should I search for the source?
Leave first. Do not operate switches, phones, plugs or appliances in the suspected area and do not try to find the leak with a flame. Make the call from a safe distance after leaving.
What if someone is still inside?

Tell the emergency responder who may be inside and the last known location. Do not reenter to search or retrieve a pet. Reentry requires the appropriate qualified clearance; disappearance of the smell is not proof of safety.
scope: Civilian educational guidance. Linked references may use U.S. emergency systems; local warning methods, laws, services and conditions differ.
